title: Mixed Quantitative — Integrated Problem Solving
tagline: Year 4 — Problems that draw on several topics at once: choosing the method before computing

introduction.overview: A real placement paper does not label questions by topic. One question is a percentage problem, the next is about trains, the next about work, and a tough one combines two of them. Integrated problem solving is the skill of recognising what a question is really asking, picking the shortest method and avoiding the topic-specific traps. This chapter practises that recognition with mixed sets in which every answer is computed.
introduction.placementRelevance: Mixed quantitative sections are how most company tests present aptitude; speed comes from recognising the type in seconds.
introduction.realWorldContext: Everyday decisions (discounts, interest, travel time, shared work) mix these same ideas.

learningObjectives: Classify a question by its structure, not its story
Choose between algebra, ratio and arithmetic methods
Combine two topics in one calculation
Check answers against the size expected

prerequisiteKnowledge.quickRefresher: Successive changes multiply; ratios share totals; speed × time = distance; work rates add; interest is on principal (simple) or on the growing balance (compound).

coreDefinitions: Structure: the mathematical shape of a problem (a ratio, a rate, a repeated change).
Successive change: changes applied one after the other, which multiply.
Rate: a quantity per unit of time or per unit of another quantity.
Consistency check: confirming units and the size of the answer.
Method choice: deciding between algebra, ratio or shortcut before computing.
conceptExplanation.theoreticalIntuition: Strip the story away and ask what the numbers do: split, grow, repeat, or race. That tells you the method.
conceptExplanation.visualOrMentalModel: Read the question once to name the structure, then write only the numbers needed. Estimate the size of the answer before computing.

mainNarrative: A shopkeeper allows 20% and then 10% off ₹800. The two discounts multiply: 800 × 0.8 × 0.9 = ₹576. A single 30% discount would give ₹560, which is wrong.
If A does a job in 12 days and B in 24, together they take 1/(1/12 + 1/24) = 8 days.
A train 240 m long crosses a pole in 12 s, so its speed is 240/12 = 20 m/s = 72 km/h.
A town of 20,000 grows 10% and then shrinks 10%: 20,000 × 1.1 × 0.9 = 19,800, a net 1% fall.
For a mixture of 40 L in the ratio 3 : 1 (milk : water), milk is 30 L. Adding 10 L of water makes the total 50 L and milk 60%.

deepDiveAspects.title: Estimate first
deepDiveAspects.content: If the answer must lie between two numbers you can compute, estimate before the full calculation to catch slips.

deepDiveAspects.title: Same story, different method
deepDiveAspects.content: A "% of a %" question is multiplication; a "how many days" question is rates; do not use the same tool for both.

solvedExamples.title: Successive discounts
solvedExamples.question: A ₹800 article is sold after discounts of 20% and 10%. Find the price.

solvedExamples.title: Combined work
solvedExamples.question: A does a job in 12 days and B in 24 days. How long together?

solvedExamples.title: Percent up then down
solvedExamples.question: A population of 20,000 grows 10% and then falls 10%. What is it now?

traditionalVsShortcut.shortcutMethod: Name the structure (split, grow, repeat, race), pick that method, and estimate the size of the answer first.

placementTips.eliminationTechnique: Reject options that are far from your estimate.
placementTips.questionSelectionAdvice: Skip a problem whose structure you cannot name in 20 seconds.
placementTips.recruiterInsight: Mixed sets reward recognition over calculation.

selfCheckQuestions: Can I name a problem's structure?
Can I choose the shortest method?
